title: Dropout: Training-Time Masking and Test-Time Weight Scaling
purpose: Show how a binary dropout mask zeroes activations during training and how the paper's test-time convention compensates by scaling weights, using a small fixed activation vector and an editable mask and retention probability.
scope: A single forward-pass activation vector with a user-supplied binary mask. We compute the masked training activation and the paper's test-time weight-scaling factor. We do not train, sample random masks, or evaluate a network.
intuition: During training, dropout randomly removes units by multiplying activations with a binary mask. At test time the paper avoids sampling by scaling the weights down by the retention probability, so the expected activation magnitude matches the training-time expectation.
learning_objectives: Compute the masked training activation from an activation vector, a binary mask, and a retention probability.
Distinguish the paper's test-time weight-scaling convention from the training-time masking and label an alternative scaling convention explicitly.
prerequisites: Expected value of a Bernoulli random variable
assumptions: The mask is a fixed user-supplied binary vector, not a random sample; it represents one possible dropout pattern.
The activation vector is a single layer's pre-dropout activations for one example.
limitations: We do not simulate the random sampling of masks or the Monte-Carlo model averaging described in the paper.
We do not train a network or measure error rates; only the forward-pass arithmetic is shown.
misconception: Dropout is often thought to scale activations at test time. In the paper's convention, test-time compensation is applied to the weights, not to the activations.
edge_cases: Retention probability p = 1 means no units are dropped and the scaling factor is 1.
A mask with all zeros removes every activation, giving a zero training activation vector.

steps.name: test_scale
steps.label: test-time weight scale
steps.meaning: The paper's test-time convention scales weights by the retention probability p, not by 1/p. This is the factor applied to weights at test time.

steps.name: alt_scale
steps.label: alternative activation scale (1/p)
steps.meaning: An alternative convention that scales activations by 1/p at test time. This is labeled as an alternative and is not the paper's weight-scaling convention.

steps.meaning: Test-time activation when weights are scaled by p; equivalently the activation is multiplied by p.

explorations.title: Baseline: moderate retention with one dropped unit
explorations.why: The mask zeroes the second unit during training. The paper's test-time convention scales weights by p = 0.8, so activations are multiplied by 0.8. The alternative convention scales activations by 1/p = 1.25, which is larger than the original activations.

explorations.title: High retention with no dropped units
explorations.why: With p close to 1, the paper's test-time scale is close to 1, so test activations are close to the original. The alternative 1/p scale is also close to 1 but slightly larger. No units are dropped, so the training activation equals the original.
